$comment: Accepted exceptions for scripts/secret-scan.mjs. Every entry needs a written justification and a path or value matcher. An entry that matches nothing is reported as stale. Never put a real credential here: only values that are public by design. Provider-key, PEM and JWT rules are never allowlisted by path alone.

allow.justification: The documented local-development PostgreSQL credentials (user and password both 'wattbyte', see infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml, apps/api/.env.example and README). The database is a throw-away container published on 127.0.0.1 only, and the same pair is used by the ephemeral service container in CI. Production credentials come from the deployment environment and are never in the repository.

The source of the scanner's own secret-name regular expression, as it was written in the first commit (SECRET_NAME = '[A-Za-z0-9_.-]*(?:secret|password|...'). It is a pattern, not a credential; only the history scan sees this old form.

Documentation example showing that a password containing '&' is kept whole by the log sanitiser (the value is the made-up string a&b followed by an unrelated query parameter); it is not a credential for any service.

Synthetic passwords, JWT signing secrets and sentinel strings used by unit and integration tests against in-memory repositories, a disposable test database or HTTP doubles. They are valid for no real service. Only the generic assignment rule is relaxed in test directories; the provider-key, PEM and JWT rules still apply there.

Fictitious URLs with a made-up user and password (hosts such as db.internal or db.example.org that never resolve) that feed the environment-validator tests in apps/api/tests/env*.test.ts and the log-redaction tests in apps/mobile/test. Nothing connects to them and they prove that such credentials are stripped from output.
Deliberately fake canary keys (the LEAKCHECK marker) that the smoke-runner tests plant in the environment to prove the real key values never appear in its output. They are not issued by any provider.

The OpenAPI exporter builds the Fastify app (which requires a JWT secret to boot) but never signs or verifies a token and never listens on a port; the value is deliberately a fixed, labelled throw-away and does not protect anything.
